newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten warns curbs on HK freedoms could backfire.
newsitem.headline: Patten warns curbs on HK freedoms could backfire.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten warned on Thursday that planned curbs on the territory's freedoms could backfire and undermine stability.

"Very often you know people produce exactly the political problems that they want to avoid when they try to slap down on people's freedoms in the name of greater stability," Patten told Reuters Television.
He said he was surprised and disappointed by plans to restrict demonstrations and foreign political links after the British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
The proposals were launched by post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa on Wednesday. He is allowing three weeks for feedback from the public in what he has called a "consultation" exercise.
"These proposals do represent a tightening of the screws on civil liberties here in Hong Kong, in what is one of the most peaceful and stable cities in the world," the governor said.
Under Sino-British agreements, Hong Kong has been guaranteed a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.
Patten refused to say whether he thought Tung was acting on orders from Beijing.
But he said the future government could show its promised autonomy by genuinely tapping the public's views on the issue.
"The voices in Hong Kong will be the same I'm sure as they have been in recent weeks," Patten said.

"And if people make it clear they want the present laws to stay, I hope Mr Tung and his colleagues will go to Peking (Beijing) and tell them that, and not impose on Hong Kong laws that people don't want," he said.
The proposals were made after China decided existing laws on public gatherings and political parties did not conform with the Basic Law, Hong Kong's post-handover constitution.
But Patten said the existing ordinances did not in any way contravene the Basic Law and that there was no justification for revising them.
